papers.title: Greater scaling and less flexible timing of cortical responses during challenging reactive balance after stroke
papers.abstract: Background: Cortical N1 responses to balance perturbations are larger and earlier with increasing magnitude and differ with reactive stepping. Whether stroke alters this modulation is unknown. Objective: To compare N1 modulation across perturbation magnitudes and reactive balance outcomes in older adults with and without stroke. We hypothesized that people with stroke would show greater N1 scaling than controls; that larger N1s at small perturbations would limit scaling (a recruitment ceiling); and that stroke would constrain N1 modulation by stepping outcome. Methods: Sixteen people with chronic stroke (66+/-11 years) and 15 age-similar controls (68+/-8 years) received forward support-surface perturbations at a small standardized magnitude and at individual step thresholds (~50% unintentional steps). N1 peak amplitude and latency were compared across magnitudes in feet-in-place trials, and between stepping and feet-in-place trials at step threshold. N1 scaling was the relative amplitude increase between magnitudes. Results: Despite lower clinical balance after stroke (p<0.001), step thresholds were similar between groups. N1s were larger with shorter latencies at step threshold in both groups (p<0.001), but scaled more after stroke (44% vs 13%,p=0.009). Greater scaling was associated with smaller small-magnitude N1s after stroke (B=0.43, p=0.041) and higher step thresholds across groups (B=0.35, p=0.048). N1 latency was 11 ms longer in stepping trials in controls but not after stroke (interaction p=0.024). Conclusions: Scaling of cortical recruitment with increasing perturbation magnitude may support reactive balance, and may be an adaptive mechanism for people after stroke. Less flexible N1 timing after stroke may limit cortical tuning to balance recovery strategy.

papers.title: Live Birth Rates Among Women With Multiple Sclerosis in Sweden, 2004 to 2022: A Population-Based Registry Study
papers.abstract: Background: Women with multiple sclerosis (MS) have fewer children than other women, but whether this narrowed as pregnancy evidence became reassuring and treatment options expanded is uncertain. Objective: To compare live birth trends from 2004 to 2022 between women with MS and all Swedish women. Methods: Linking the Swedish MS, National Patient, and Medical Birth Registers with national statistics, we compared age-standardised live birth rates, counted expected births at national rates, and estimated adjusted annual live-birth risk ratios in a matched comparison sample. Results: Women with MS (n=10,452; 76,989 woman-years) had 3,577 children, about 1,200 (25%) fewer than expected (observed-to-expected ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.77). Standardised rate ratios were below 1 annually (median 0.77). Observed-to-expected ratios were 0.73 (0.68 to 0.79) in 2004 to 2008 and 0.70 (0.65 to 0.75) in 2019 to 2022 (population-by-period interaction p=0.31). Age- and region-adjusted risk ratios ranged from 0.75 to 0.86 across periods (heterogeneity p=0.020), closest to 1 in 2009 to 2013. Conclusion: Women with MS had about one quarter fewer live births than other Swedish women, and the difference was similar in the first and last periods.

papers.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy and Disability Progression in Women with Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background: Evidence on menopausal hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and disability progression in women with multiple sclerosis (MS) is limited, particularly in the era of high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy. We estimated the association between systemic HRT and sustained disability progression and recurring relapses in a contemporary national cohort. Methods: In a nationwide Swedish registry-based cohort, we followed women with MS aged 40 to 60 years entering from 2006 through 2024, with follow-up through 2025, under a new-user design. Systemic HRT was modeled as time-varying current use and quarterly oral-equivalent dose categories. Outcomes were sustained Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) 4.0, sustained EDSS 6.0, and recurring relapses. Cox models adjusted for baseline covariates and time-varying age and disease-modifying therapy (DMT) class. Results: Among 7,623 women, 1,192 (15.6%) initiated HRT. Current HRT use was associated with a lower hazard of sustained EDSS 4.0 (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 0.96) but not sustained EDSS 6.0 (aHR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.16) or recurring relapses (aHR 1.00, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.36). Dose categories showed no consistent gradient. Raising the cohort-entry age floor to 50 years gave a consistent EDSS 4.0 estimate (aHR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.95). Conclusions: HRT was not associated with increased relapse risk or severe disability progression. The lower hazard of sustained EDSS 4.0 was not mirrored at EDSS 6.0 and showed no dose gradient. Given menopausal status was unmeasured, replication in cohorts with verified menopausal status is required for clear clinical interpretation.

papers.title: More tests, higher scores: Testing frequency and SDMT differences between natalizumab and rituximab
papers.abstract: Background: The Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) measures information processing speed, and repeated testing can increase scores through practice effects. However, how differences in testing frequency bear on comparisons between disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) in real-world cohorts has not been fully explored. Objective: To compare SDMT trajectories between natalizumab and rituximab users and quantify the association of the testing process with those trajectories. Methods: Using the Swedish MS Registry, we studied adults with relapsing-remitting MS initiating natalizumab or rituximab (2010-2024) with >=2 on-treatment SDMT assessments. Mixed-effects models with restricted cubic spline time were sequentially adjusted; log cumulative test number was the practice-effect adjustment. Results: Among 2,458 individuals, natalizumab initiators were tested twice as often as rituximab initiators (1.6 vs. 0.8 tests/year). The predicted natalizumab-minus-rituximab SDMT difference at 3 years was 7.0 points (95% CI 5.7-8.3) unadjusted and 1.6 (0.7-2.6) after full adjustment including cumulative test number; at 1 year it fell from 4.4 (3.3-5.4) to -0.3 (-1.2 to 0.6). Conclusion: Adjustment for cumulative test number substantially attenuated the SDMT difference between natalizumab and rituximab, leaving a small residual difference of uncertain clinical importance and underscoring the need to account for testing frequency in real-world comparisons.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

papers.title: EEG Biomarkers for Rett Syndrome: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by abnormal cortical activity, which can be captured using electroencephalography (EEG). Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise for diagnosing several neurological conditions, comprehensive evaluation of classical ML and deep learning (DL) methods, together with physiologically meaningful explanations, remains limited for RTT. This study analyses resting-state, eyes-closed EEG recordings from RTT patients and healthy controls using both power spectral density (PSD)-based ML and end-to-end DL frameworks. Classical ML models, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were trained on PSD features, while EEG-specific DL architectures, including ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, EEGNet, and EEG Conformer, were trained directly on preprocessed EEG signals. Subject-wise cross-validation was used to avoid data leakage, with balanced accuracy as the primary performance metric because it equally accounts for sensitivity and specificity. Random Forest achieved the best performance among the classical ML models, whereas EEGNet achieved the highest DL performance. An ablation study indicated that 4-second EEG epochs offered the optimal trade-off between model performance and robustness. Model interpretability was investigated using SHAP for Random Forest and occlusion sensitivity analysis for EEGNet. Both methods consistently identified delta and theta oscillations, along with centro-frontal brain regions, as key contributors to RTT classification. These findings show that both PSD-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning methods can reliably identify RTT and highlight common neurophysiological biomarkers, offering an interpretable framework for EEG-based diagnosis and biomarker discovery for Rett Syndrome.

papers.title: Cortical physiological arousal following termination of absence seizures
papers.abstract: Although the brain state preceding and during absence seizures has been well-characterized, the postictal brain state remains largely unexplored due to the prevailing assumption that absence seizures have minimal or no postictal changes. To address this gap, scalp EEG recordings from 55 patients with 3-4 Hz spike-wave discharges across four multi-site cohorts were analyzed. Spectral power was measured relative to each seizure's preictal baseline, and the postictal period was compared to a time-matched preictal window. Rather than an immediate return to baseline after seizure offset, a significant broadband increase in EEG power was observed in the gamma (>25 Hz) and delta (<4 Hz) frequency bands, followed by a gradual decline over the next 15 s to 30 s. In contrast, no comparable change preceded the seizures. This suggests that recovery from an absence seizure is an active process with a characteristic electrophysiological signature consistent with cortical activation and arousal. Thus, postictal arousal may facilitate exit from the seizure state, and with further work could serve as an electrophysiological marker and therapeutic target for recovery in absence epilepsy.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Across Sleep Disorders and Its Cognitive Implications
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), sleep deprivation (SD), and narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), are associated with cognitive dysfunction and an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease. Glymphatic transport disruption has been suggested as one potential mechanistic link. However, evidence across sleep disorders and glymphatic-related metrics remains fragmented. We aimed to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical and preclinical studies to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. Across studies of OSA, glymphatic-related metrics indicated significant impairment of glymphatic transport with a moderate negative association between apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index (r=-0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.63 to -0.41; p<0.001). Available evidence did not demonstrate statistically significant alterations in glymphatic measures in SD or NT1. These findings suggest that impaired glymphatic transport may represent a potential pathway linking OSA to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative risk. However, current evidence is insufficient to determine whether comparable alterations occur in SD or NT1. Substantial heterogeneity across studies highlights the need for standardized reporting and harmonized methodologies to advance the field.

papers.title: Movement-specific effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation over premotor and parietal cortices after stroke
papers.abstract: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been proposed to support post-stroke motor recovery, but the response may depend on the task and motor-network status. We aimed to compare how premotor and parietal stimulation affects performance across reach directions with different movement demands, in preparation for therapeutic application of TMS. Methods: 16 participants with chronic subcortical stroke performed planar reaches with the KINARM exoskeleton toward distal and proximal targets. Before movement, a 10-Hz triple-pulse TMS train was delivered over bilateral dorsal or ventral premotor cortex (PMd, PMv) or dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (PPC) at subthreshold and suprathreshold intensities. The parietal midline was used as the control target. Participant-level bootstrap confidence intervals assessed changes in trajectory straightness and smoothness relative to the control target and differences between reach directions. We compared motor-network activity and connectivity using task-based and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from participants with stroke and neurologically intact controls. To explore response variability, we tested associations between TMS response and motor impairment, resting-state connectivity, and the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement. Results: Suprathreshold PMd and PPC stimulation in both hemispheres improved trajectory straightness or smoothness during distal reaches relative to the control target. Suprathreshold contralesional PMd stimulation increased trajectory deviation and reduced smoothness during proximal reaches. Baseline performance during distal reaches was more closely related to motor impairment, and contralesional PMd effects were more favorable during distal than proximal reaches across all kinematic measures. Participants with stroke showed lower bilateral PMv activation during movement and stronger interhemispheric PPC connectivity. Only the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement was related to TMS response. Smaller changes relative to controls were associated with more favorable kinematic effects during distal reaches. Conclusions: Movements more affected after stroke were the most responsive to this type of stimulation. The response to TMS was also associated with task-evoked activity differences at the stimulated region between movement planning and execution. Neuromodulation may therefore be most effective when designed around both the pathophysiology of the cortical target and the type of movement.

papers.title: Amyloid and Tau Neuropathologic Stage, Coexisting Brain Disease, and Cognitive Status in a Population-Based Autopsy Cohort
papers.abstract: Importance: Interpreting an amyloid or tau biomarker result requires knowing how often the target pathology is present in the tested population, whether a single marker characterizes the joint amyloid-tau state, and whether the detected pathology explains the patient symptoms. Population-based autopsy data addressing these questions are scarce, and recent population-scale prevalence estimates rest on biomarkers rather than ground-truth tissue examination. Objective: To estimate stage-resolved, age- and sex-specific frequencies of amyloid and tau neuropathology in an unselected, admixed, autopsy population and to evaluate their clinical expression in relation to coexisting neuropathology. Design Setting and Participants: Cross-sectional clinicopathologic study of decedents accrued from 2004 through 2025 at the Biobank for Aging Studies of the University of Sao Paulo, sampled through the centralized Sao Paulo municipal autopsy service, which performs approximately 15 000 autopsies annually and verifies about 16% of deaths in the city. Eligible decedents were aged 18 years or older with complete amyloid, tau, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and coexisting pathology assessments. Exposures: Age, sex, Thal amyloid phase, Braak neurofibrillary tangle stage, Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque score, and contributing coexisting neuropathology. Main Outcomes and Measures: The complete Thal phase by Braak stage distribution; age- and sex-specific frequency of pathology in the biomarker-detectable range, prespecified as Thal phase 3 to 5 together with Braak stage IV to VI; and associations with CDR and CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB). Results: Among 2711 decedents (mean [SD] age, 73.4 [14.4] years; range, 23 to 111 years; 1340 [49.4%] female), 531 (19.6%) met both thresholds, 270 (10.0%) the amyloid threshold only, 207 (7.6%) the tau threshold only, and 1703 (62.8%) neither. Frequency of the combined state rose from 0% at ages 23 to 50 years to 5.5% at 61 to 70, 14.5% at 71 to 80, 36.5% at 81 to 90, and 45.9% at 91 to 111 years. The proportion with CDR greater than 0 increased monotonically across Braak stages, from 88 of 541 (16.3%) at stage 0 to 155 of 179 (86.6%) at stage VI. When the combined amyloid-tau state was cross-classified with contributing coexisting pathology, CDR greater than 0 was present in 225 of 1467 participants (15.3%) with neither, 204 of 349 (58.5%) with coexisting pathology alone, 216 of 339 (63.7%) with combined amyloid-tau pathology alone, and 165 of 192 (85.9%) with both. In a multivariable model of CDR-SB, contributing coexisting pathology had the largest unique adjusted contribution (partial R2, 0.088; 95% CI, 0.064-0.114), and Braak stage had the largest share of total explained variance (Lindeman, Merenda, and Gold contribution, 0.115). Conclusions and Relevance: Amyloid and tau pathology within the range detected by current biomarkers was uncommon before age 70 and discordant in 17.6% of decedents. Contributing coexisting brain disease, which amyloid and tau biomarkers do not detect, accompanied cognitive impairment as often as advanced Alzheimer disease pathology did. These tissue-based frequencies can inform the interpretation of positive and negative biomarker results.

papers.title: High-Density Surface Electromyography Detects Fiber-Type-Related Profiles and Disease-Relevant Fatigue Trajectories in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Fiber-type composition contributes to contractile behavior and fatigue resistance. Characterizing these physiological differences could help study and monitor disease-related changes. Direct fiber-type measurement requires biopsy, whereas animal findings may not fully translate to humans. High-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) may offer repeatable, noninvasive assessment. We recorded HD-sEMG from tibialis anterior (TA) and soleus, muscles with contrasting fast- and slow-twitch-like physiology, during sustained contractions at 30% and 50% maximum voluntary contraction in participants with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; n = 7) and healthy controls (n = 10). Given fast-fatigable motor unit vulnerability in ALS models, we compared TA-soleus profiles and fatigue-related changes. Amplitude, spectral, motor unit firing, and motor unit action potential (MUAP) features were quantified in the first 10 s of stable contraction, with firing and MUAP features derived from decomposition. Exploratory fatigue analyses assessed early-to-late changes and trajectories. Early-window root mean square (RMS), spectral power, firing rate, and MUAP amplitude were higher in TA than soleus in both groups. Group x Muscle interactions were nonsignificant. Despite higher early values, TA showed larger fatigue-related declines in high-frequency power, RMS, and firing rate than soleus, particularly in ALS-affected TA. These findings suggest HD-sEMG detects muscle-type-related electrophysiological differences, with ALS-related changes more evident during fatigue.

papers.title: APOLLAI, a multimodal AI system, versus EMS personnel for prehospital detection of stroke-related deficits
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Prehospital stroke recognition remains suboptimal, with nearly one-third of strokes unidentified before hospital arrival, and neurological assessment being inherently subjective, with substantial interobserver variability even among certified clinicians. APOLLAI, a multimodal artificial intelligence system, was developed to detect stroke-related neurological deficits from video and audio recordings. We compared the diagnostic performance of APOLLAI and emergency medical services (EMS) personnel against an expert consensus reference standard. Methods: In this prospective study, video recordings of 295 patients with suspected stroke (mean age, 70.3 {+/-}13.3 years) were obtained at Nimes University Hospital (August 2023-July 2025). Five National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale items (best gaze, facial palsy, motor arm, aphasia, dysarthria) were independently annotated by seven certified stroke neurologists, combined into consensus labels using the Dawid-Skene algorithm, and separately assessed by EMS personnel (mean of 15 raters per patient). APOLLAI, a multimodal machine-learning framework that combines computer vision, audio-based deep learning, and a final support vector machine (SVM) fusion classifier, was evaluated against EMS using sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results: Interrater agreement among the seven neurologists was moderate overall (mean {kappa}=0.541, range, 0.367-0.732), indicating an intrinsic difficulty of neurological assessment. APOLLAI showed higher sensitivity than EMS for all five neurological tasks and for the global assessment (78.5% versus 59.4%), with broadly comparable specificity (87.0% versus 85.9% for the global assessment). AUC values ranged from 0.839 (facial palsy) to 0.966 (best gaze), with a global AUC of 0.882. Conclusions: APOLLAI demonstrated higher sensitivity than EMS personnel for detecting stroke-related neurological deficits, with preserved specificity. These findings support its potential as a standardized, scalable adjunct to prehospital stroke recognition, warranting prospective validation under real-world EMS conditions.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomic Classification of Alzheimer Disease, Parkinson Disease, and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Using a Single Neurodegeneration Panel: A Diagnostic Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Importance: Blood biomarkers for Alzheimer disease(AD), Parkinson disease(PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis(ALS) are typically developed as disease-specific single-analyte tests. Whether one shared plasma panel can support disease-selective classification remains unclear. Objective: To test whether the Olink Target 48 Neurodegeneration plasma panel, analyzed with disease-specific Elastic Net models, can discriminate AD, PD, and ALS in a heterogeneous neurological cohort. Design, Setting, and Participants: Single-center diagnostic cohort study at Keio University Hospital, Tokyo, Japan. After quality control and one consent withdrawal, 302 participants were analyzed(healthy controls n = 62; AD continuum n = 93; PD n = 39; ALS n = 27; other neurological disorders n = 81) and allocated by diagnosis-stratified sampling into a discovery training set(n = 211) and a locked hold-out test set(n = 91). Exposures: Plasma normalized protein expression from 42 assays retained after protein quality control. Plasma DOPA decarboxylase was excluded a priori from all classifiers because blood levels primarily reflect dopaminergic treatment exposure. Main Outcomes and Measures: Hold-out receiver operating characteristic area under the curve(AUC). Sensitivity and specificity at a training-set Youden threshold locked for Test. Results: Hold-out AUCs were 0.974(95% CI, 0.942-0.995) for AD, 0.926(0.820-1.000) for PD, and 0.995(0.980-1.000) for ALS. At locked Youden cutoffs, sensitivity was 0.929 (95% CI, 0.765-0.991) and specificity was 0.921 (95% CI, 0.824-0.974) for AD, 0.833 (95% CI, 0.516-0.979) and 0.975 (95% CI, 0.912-0.997) for PD, and 1.000 (95% CI, 0.631-1.000) and 0.940 (95% CI, 0.865-0.980) for ALS. Conclusions and Relevance: A single plasma neurodegeneration panel supported disease-selective classification of AD, PD, and ALS in internal validation. Multicenter external validation is needed before clinical application.

papers.title: Sensorimotor cortex activity during cued gait differs in Parkinson's freezers and non-freezers
papers.abstract: Gait impairments are a major contributor to disability in patients with Parkinson's disease despite dopaminergic and neuromodulation therapies. External cues (e.g., visual targets, rhythmic auditory sounds) are commonly used to improve gait quality and reduce freezing of gait (FOG), yet their effectiveness varies across patients and contexts. Improved understanding of the neural mechanisms of cueing benefits is essential to personalize rehabilitation strategies and improve outcomes. We use mobile electroencephalography (EEG) to test the hypothesis that cues improve gait through engagement of voluntary motor control mechanisms to compensate for impaired gait automaticity. In addition, we investigate whether this mechanism is related to cueing benefits or freezing status. Eighteen PD patients with a history of freezing (PD-F), 21 patients without freezing (PD-NF) and 19 age-matched healthy controls (HC) walked overground under three conditions: normal walking, synchronizing to auditory cues, and stepping over visual cues. Stride-locked beta band (13-30 Hz) power dynamics in sensorimotor cortex were used to measure cortical control of stepping. Spatiotemporal gait parameters improved with cues in all groups. However, PD-F had smaller cue-related gains in speed and stride length when compared with PD-NF for both cue types, and did not improve gait speed with visual cues. EEG revealed greater contralateral sensorimotor cortex swing-phase beta suppression in PD-F than PD-NF patients, with visual cues eliciting the most robust response. In contrast, beta suppression with cues was less pronounced in PD-NF and HC, despite greater behavioral gains. In addition, engagement of sensorimotor cortex during visual cueing was associated with divergent gait effects across PD subgroups: In PD-NF greater beta suppression was associated with less gait improvement, whereas in PD-F the opposite was observed. These findings suggest distinct sensorimotor control mechanisms for cue utilization in PD-F and PD-NF, and indicate that engagement of voluntary motor control circuits may underlie cueing benefits primarily in PD-F.

papers.title: Near infrared spectroscopy during non-ischaemic handgrip exercise reveals divergent muscle oxygenation signatures in mitochondrial disease and sarcopenia
papers.abstract: Background: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of ageing and is implicated in the pathogenesis of sarcopenia. Genetically confirmed mitochondrial disease provides a biologically definitive model of impaired oxidative phosphorylation against which novel functional assessments can be validated. We investigated whether a brief, submaximal, non-ischaemic intermittent isometric handgrip exercise protocol combined with Near Infra-Red Spectroscopy (NIRS) could detect distinct muscle oxygenation signatures in mitochondrial disease and sarcopenia. Methods: Adults with genetically confirmed mitochondrial disease (n=10, 7 female) and group-matched controls (n=19, 11 female), underwent assessment of maximal grip force, handgrip relaxation kinetics and a 3-minute intermittent submaximal isometric handgrip test (40% maximal voluntary contraction, 1Hz contraction/relaxation) with continuous force recording at 2000Hz and simultaneous NIRS. Findings were compared with 23 community-dwelling older adults from the Muscle Ageing and Sarcopenia Study (MASS) Lifecourse cohort (n=23, 13 female) including seven with probable or confirmed sarcopenia according to European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2) criteria. Results: Participants with mitochondrial disease demonstrated an attenuated reduction in tissue saturation index (TSI) during exercise compared with controls (TSI % {middle dot} s150-180s: -59.9 {+/-} 94.5 vs -175.1 {+/-} 128.4; p=0.02). Total haemoglobin (THb) responses did not differ between groups (p=0.10). In contrast, participants with probable or confirmed sarcopenia showed exaggerated reduction in TSI compared with non-sarcopenic participants (TSI % {middle dot} s150-180s: -256.5 {+/-} 146.0 vs -121.2 {+/-} 95.2; p=0.05), while THb responses remained similar. The association between sarcopenia and TSI differed by sex (interaction coefficient -240, p=0.016), with greater TSI reductions observed in males with sarcopenia. Differences in TSI between mitochondrial disease and control groups were independent of age and sex. No statistically significant associations were observed between THb responses and age, sex or force production. Conclusions: A brief, non-ischaemic handgrip exercise protocol combined with NIRS identified divergent muscle oxygenation responses in mitochondrial disease and sarcopenia. The attenuated TSI response observed in genetically confirmed mitochondrial disease is consistent with impaired oxygen utilisation secondary to defective oxidative phosphorylation, whereas the exaggerated TSI reduction observed in sarcopenia suggests a distinct physiological mechanism, potentially involving impaired oxygen delivery, reduced muscle efficiency, or both. This portable and non-invasive approach has significant potential as a physiological biomarker for mechanistic studies and clinical trials in ageing and neuromuscular disease. More broadly, our findings demonstrate how biologically defined rare diseases can provide a powerful framework for interpreting mechanisms in common heterogeneous age-related conditions.

papers.title: AI Tools to Assist with Management of Patient Portal Messages: Auto-Categorization and Routing
papers.abstract: Background and Objective: The volume of patient portal messages has grown substantially and artificial intelligence (AI) can support clinical staff and improve the timeliness of patient care. Our objective is to test if an AI tool for managing the electronic inbox In-Basket reduces response times to patient portal messages in neurology. Methods: We conducted an implementation study from January to May 2026 in the neurology department at two clinical sites within a regional medical system. A single AI tool was implemented to auto-categorize and auto-route all patient messages received in the electronic inbox. The tool also generates optional draft replies to messages. Primary process measures were the median weekly time (hours) from message creation to the first action and to closure. Impact was analyzed using a controlled interrupted time-series (ITS) design, comparing message-volume-matched control divisions. Results: Among 24,142 messages analyzed, pre-intervention median weekly time to first action was 11.3 hours [IQR: 5.6, 15.1] (Site A) and 16.1 hours [IQR: 13.8, 19.0] (Site B), falling post-intervention to 1.0 hour [IQR: 0, 3.1] (Site A) and 0.6 hours [IQR: 0.2, 2.4] (Site B). Controlled interrupted time-series analysis showed a significant immediate differential level change in median weekly hours to first action at Site A (-92.5%, 95% CI: -97.5% to -78.0%), and a significant downward trend at Site B (-43.5%, 95% CI: -65.2% to -8.2%). Changes in time to closure were directionally favorable but not statistically significant at either site. There was low use of the generated draft replies, only 0.5% at Site A and 3% at Site B. Discussion: Implementation of AI-assisted message categorization and routing was associated with a substantially reduced initial action time for patient In-Basket messages in Epilepsy. The utilization of AI-generated draft-replies to messages was low. These findings support the feasibility and effectiveness of AI-augmented workflows to improve inbox management.

papers.title: Fibromyalgia, Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, and Multiple Sclerosis are associated with lower translocator protein binding affinity genotypes
papers.abstract: Introduction: Neuroinflammation is a known pathophysiologic mechanism in multiple sclerosis and a proposed mechanism in fibromyalgia and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging of the translocator protein (TSPO) has been widely used to measure neuroinflammation, though second-generation ligands are highly sensitive to a single nucleotide polymorphism, rs6971, resulting in high, mixed, and low affinity binders. It is unknown whether this polymorphism is associated with neuroinflammatory disorders. Materials and Methods: Eighty-six total participant genotypes for TSPO binding affinity were identified through Sanger sequencing (30 fibromyalgia, 21 ME/CFS, 11 multiple sclerosis, and 24 healthy controls). Associations between patient group and genotype were assessed with Fishers Exact test. Associations between genotype and symptom severity from self-report questionnaires were assessed with Kruskal-Wallis tests. Results: In the present study individuals with fibromyalgia, (ME/CFS), or multiple sclerosis were more likely to have a mixed- or low-affinity genotypes compared to healthy controls. Presence of the low or mixed genotypes were also associated with greater self-reported fatigue severity and depressive symptoms. Discussion: These findings should be confirmed in larger samples but suggest functional consequences of rs6971 polymorphism that may be related to the pathophysiology of pain and fatigue illnesses.

papers.title: Quantifying statistical power gains from prognostic modeling in Huntington's Disease
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives Huntington's disease is a rare neurodegenerative disease in which optimizing clinical trial design is essential. Although baseline characteristics are known to predict disease progression, the statistical efficiency gains achievable by formally integrating prognostic predictions into trial analyses have not been systematically quantified. We aimed to benchmark prognostic modeling approaches, quantify the trial efficiency gains from prognostic covariate adjustment, and deliver a ready-to-deploy framework for immediate implementation. Methods: We developed a two-step modeling pipeline using longitudinal Enroll-HD natural history data (NCT01574053) to train nine machine learning algorithms to predict disease progression across five UHDRS endpoints. For this, we used 16 predictive baseline covariates representing stage of disease (baseline score levels), disease specific (CAP, CAG length), demographics and co-medication use that could be quantified in one clinical visit. For Total Function Capacity (TFC), frequently used as a primary endpoint in clinical trials, we also devised a minimal prognostic model based on 6 covariates. Model performance was tested using the placebo arm of the GENERATION HD1 phase 3 trial (NCT03761849). Results: Models were trained on 16,398 Enroll-HD participants and tested on 260 participants from the GENERATION HD1 placebo arm. Models that take into account nonlinear relationships between the covariates showed no performance advantage over linear-based models on the test set. For TFC, a minimal six-covariate linear prognostic model performed on par with the full 16-feature model. Adjusting for the prognostic score increased the signal-to-noise ratio across different trial visits by 8-18%, raising statistical power from 80% to up to 90% at a fixed sample size, or, equivalently, reducing required sample size by 15-28% compared to unadjusted analyses (no covariate adjustment). Compared to routinely used covariate adjustments (including baseline score, age, CAG repeat length, and CAP score), adjusting for a prognostic score consistently delivered meaningful additional efficiency gains. Discussion: Prognostic covariate adjustment using a simple six-covariate linear score derived from a single baseline visit yields meaningful gains in statistical power for HD clinical trials, while remaining fully embedded within standard, regulator-accepted analysis frameworks. This approach offers a practical and immediately deployable tool to improve trial design.

papers.title: Association Between Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio and Cardiac Sympathetic Denervation in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Background: Peripheral inflammation has been implicated in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), but its relationship with autonomic dysfunction remains unclear. Objectives: To explore the association between peripheral inflammation, assessed by the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and autonomic function in patients with PD. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 97 patients with PD who underwent 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy and differential blood cell counts. Associations of NLR with early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios, washout ratio, and the coefficient of variation of R-R intervals (CVRR) were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation and multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and disease duration. Results: No significant univariable correlations were observed between NLR and the autonomic measures. In multivariable analysis, higher NLR was associated with a lower early H/M ratio (B = -0.802, 95% CI -1.598 to -0.005, P = 0.049), whereas no significant associations were observed with the delayed H/M ratio, washout ratio, or CVRR. Sensitivity analyses showed a generally consistent direction of association, although the effect estimate was attenuated after exclusion of two influential observations and statistical significance was not consistently retained. Conclusions: Higher NLR was associated with lower early cardiac MIBG uptake after adjustment for age, sex, and disease duration in patients with PD. This exploratory finding raises the possibility of an association between systemic inflammation and sympathetic dysfunction in PD and requires confirmation in larger prospective studies.

papers.title: Plasma biomarkers and incident clinical stage progression in the specialized memory clinic: a longitudinal study
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The utility of blood-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers in predicting clinical trajectories remains uncertain. METHODS: We assessed the diagnostic and prognostic performance of p-tau181, p-tau217, GFAP, and NfL in a large memory-clinic cohort (n=3,645) with comprehensive baseline clinical evaluation and annual follow-up for up to three decades. RESULTS: P-tau217, p-tau181 and GFAP were associated with amyloid-beta (A{beta}) pathology, while all biomarkers were elevated in AD and all-cause dementia. P-tau217 significantly outperformed others in detecting A{beta} pathology and clinical AD but performed similarly to NfL and GFAP for all-cause dementia. Prognostically, p-tau217 demonstrated the strongest association with cognitive decline, followed by GFAP and NfL, and best predicted progression status at 5- and 10-year intervals. All biomarkers provided added prognostic value beyond demographic and genetic covariates. DISCUSSION: These findings support plasma biomarkers for disease identification and risk stratification while underscoring the need for population-specific approaches.

papers.title: Feature harmonization reveals that apparent cross-cohort differences in tau-positivity prediction reflect variable availability and cohort stage structure
papers.abstract: Background: Cross-cohort machine-learning studies of tau positivity are increasingly used to assess generalizability of Alzheimer's disease biomarker models, but apparent differences between cohorts may reflect clinical severity structure and cohort stage composition rather than genuine biological divergence. Methods: We evaluated this problem across subject-level cohorts from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS3), and the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) using harmonized tabular predictors and a feature-block ablation framework. For ADNI and OASIS3, we performed matched-feature analyses restricted to shared harmonized variables (age, APOE e4, education, sex, the CDR(R) Dementia Staging Instrument sum-of-boxes score (CDR-SB), and the Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ)). Models were trained with five-fold stratified cross-validation using balanced logistic regression as the primary classifier. Random forests and extra-trees classifiers were evaluated as robustness checks and are reported in supplementary analyses. Results: In the primary matched-feature comparison, reference areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.851 for ADNI tau90, 0.860 for ADNI tau180, and 0.933 for OASIS3 tau180. Severity-only models retained 86-99% of reference performance, whereas demographic/genetic-only models retained 85-87%; bootstrap confidence intervals showed that the reference-minus-demo contrast remained positive across all primary cohorts. Before feature matching, OASIS3 showed substantially weaker demographic-only prediction (AUC approx. 0.54), attributable to missing APOE and age variables. After harmonization with a matched feature set including age, the pre-harmonization demographic gap was no longer attributable to feature availability; the residual difference was most consistent with cohort disease-stage composition asymmetry, with CDR-SB = 0 prevalence of 84.5-88.7% in OASIS3 versus 49.3-51.7% in ADNI. Conclusions: The original large ADNI-OASIS3 performance gap was largely a feature-availability artifact; after strict harmonization including age-field repair, the absolute gap narrowed and the signed ADNI-minus-OASIS3 difference reversed, with the residual difference most consistent with cohort disease-stage composition asymmetry. Clinical severity remains an important predictor across all cohorts, but the unique contributions of severity and demographic/genetic information depend strongly on stage composition. Cross-cohort biomarker modeling should account for both feature-set completeness and disease-stage composition heterogeneity, not only headline performance metrics.

papers.title: Biological age measured by DNA methylation clocks and neurodegenerative diseases: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Hallmarks of biological ageing are closely interconnected with neurodegenerative diseases. Deoxyribonucleic acid methylation (DNAm) clocks quantify biological age and may serve as peripheral biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to examine associations between DNAm-based biological age metrics and neurodegenerative diseases. Six databases were systematically searched from 1st January 2011 to 15th April 2026 for studies reporting associations between DNAm-based ages and neurodegenerative diseases including all-cause dementia, Parkinson's Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. Correlated-and-hierarchical-effects meta-analyses were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood with Knapp-Hartung adjustment. Of 42,023 records screened, 37 observational studies (n=46365; 60.5% female; median of mean age 69.4 years [IQR 62.5-73.3)) and seven Mendelian randomization studies met inclusion criteria. In longitudinal meta-analyses, higher GrimAge epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) was significantly associated with higher dementia risk (HR per SD 1.11 [95% CI 1.02-1.20]; I^2 = 0.0%; p = 0.018), whereas Horvath1 EAA, Hannum EAA, PhenoAge EAA, and DunedinPACE were not significantly associated with dementia risk. Evidence for other neurodegenerative diseases were heterogeneous across clock generations and study designs. Mendelian randomization provided limited evidence for causality. Higher GrimAge EAA was the only DNAm age measure consistently predictive of higher all-cause dementia risk. Overall, however, DNAm age clocks show limited and inconsistent associations with neurodegenerative diseases, providing insufficient support for their use as disease biomarkers. These findings highlight the need to develop and independently validate disease-specific DNAm clocks and undertake pathway analyses to identify methylation changes associated with neurodegeneration and the biological processes they reflect.

papers.title: Predictive modeling for stroke using routine clinical and socio-demographic data in Uganda
papers.abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of mortality and disability in Uganda, with a prevalence of approximately 2.5% and a 25-30% 30-day mortality rate, exacerbated by limited access to predictive tools and advanced diagnostics. Machine learning (ML) offers potential for early stroke risk stratification, but its application in resource-constrained settings like Uganda requires tailored models and rigorous performance evaluation, as well as assessment of misclassification patterns. This study aimed to develop and internally validate an ML-based predictive model for stroke using clinical and socio-demographic characteristics among patients at Mulago National Referral Hospital (MNRH) and residents of Wakiso District, Uganda, identify key predictors and assess misclassification patterns to enhance targeted prevention. A retrospective case-control study utilized secondary data from 1,016 participants (254 stroke cases, 762 controls) across three prior studies conducted between 2006 and 2015. Eight ML algorithms were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation, with performance metrics including accuracy, sensitivity, positive predictive value, F1-score, and area under receiver operator characteristics curve (AU-ROC). McNemars test compared model classification performance of the top 2 models. Feature importance identified key predictors, and misclassification patterns were analyzed using classification matrix and line graphs. The Random Forest (RF) model achieved the highest performance (95.18% accuracy, 90.10% F1-score, 97% AU-ROC). McNemars test confirmed RFs superior classification (p=0.01). Age, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, and waist-hip ratio were the top drivers of RF stroke predictions. RF misclassified 8.3% of stroke cases and 3.3% of non-stroke cases, due to overlaps in risk profiles (e.g., lower cholesterol, systolic blood pressure and age in false negatives). The RF model demonstrates strong potential for stroke risk prediction in Uganda, leveraging routine data to prioritize high-risk individuals. Misclassification analysis highlights areas for model refinement, supporting its potential for integration into clinical workflows for early intervention and stroke prevention in resource-limited settings. Future external validation across diverse populations is recommended.

papers.title: Concussion, Attention, and Mental Health: A Brain Network Study in Youth (CAMBY) - Study Protocol
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDOne in three adolescents with a concussion history report experiencing long-lasting somatic, sleep, emotional, and/or cognitive disturbances (persisting symptoms after concussion (PSaC)). Cognitive difficulties, such as attentional problems, are common symptoms and can interfere with ongoing development. Clinically, psychiatric symptoms also present in youth with PSaC. A concussion causes diffuse functional and microstructural alterations to neural networks. To develop targeted treatments for PSaC (e.g., neurostimulation), we need to understand how and where structural alterations and neural dysfunction intersect to cause long-lasting symptoms. OBJECTIVES1) Identify functional and microstructural properties in intrinsic connectivity networks, as well as neuropsychological outcomes, that differentiate adolescents with concussion with PSaC from those who do not have PSaC. 2) Determine whether neural activity within intrinsic connectivity networks mediates the relationship between network microstructure and specific neuropsychological features in adolescents with concussion. METHODSCAMBY is a prospective study of adolescents aged 12 to 18 years with a history of concussion. Participants are allocated based on recovery status (PSaC vs. No-PSaC (recovered controls)). Advanced structural (magnetic resonance imaging; MRI) and functional (magnetoencephalography; MEG) neuroimaging and neuropsychological measures will be collected one month or more after concussion. Microstructural and functional features will be computed within intrinsic connectivity networks, then compared between PSaC and recovered control groups and related to symptom domains and neuropsychological profiles. IMPACTThis will be the first study to integrate MRI, MEG, and neuropsychology in adolescents with PSaC to identify disrupted networks underlying PSaC. This observational study is a necessary step towards future clinical trials that accurately target promising therapeutic neurostimulation protocols.

papers.title: APOE ε4 Modifies the Association of Left Atrial Remodeling With Brain Aging
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONWhether APOE {varepsilon}4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown. METHODSIn Framingham Heart Study Offspring participants, we related antecedent echocardiographic remodeling (Examinations 4-6) to repeated brain MRI, and cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes to regional cortical morphometry, testing cardiac x APOE {varepsilon}4 interactions with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction and permutation testing of the regional screen. RESULTSAPOE {varepsilon}4 modified the association between antecedent left atrial (LA) remodeling and subsequent lateral ventricular expansion ({beta}=-0.00858, P=1.45x10-, q=0.0023; N=1,305; 3,787 MRI observations), the only FDR-significant result of 16 longitudinal tests, including with participant-specific MRI-time slopes (q=0.034); it weakened when intracranial volume x MRI time was modeled. Four regional ventricular cardiac x APOE {varepsilon}4 interactions met within-family FDR criteria, but their number was consistent with chance (permutation P=0.70). Maximum LA volume index showed an APOE {varepsilon}4-dependent association with left middle-occipital cortical-thickness variability (whole-brain q=0.017; permutation P=0.041) that persisted after ventricular adjustment. Cardiac phenotypes and trajectories showed no FDR-significant APOE {varepsilon}4-dependent associations with plasma A{beta}42/40, p-tau181, GFAP, or NfL, and adjustment for these biomarkers changed the regional interactions by at most 3.2%. Allen Human Brain Atlas data showed cholesterol-biosynthesis enrichment in the right superior frontal cortex, implicated by the LV end-systolic volume interaction, but without convergent pathway evidence. DISCUSSIONAPOE {varepsilon}4 modified atrial-brain relationships, with the strongest evidence linking antecedent atrial remodeling to later ventricular expansion. Replication with prespecified models is needed. HighlightsO_LIAPOE {varepsilon}4 modified how left atrial remodeling related to later brain ventricle growth. C_LIO_LIIt was the only FDR-significant result of 16 tests and persisted with random slopes. C_LIO_LIIn {varepsilon}4 carriers, larger LA volume tracked lower occipital thickness variability. C_LIO_LIThis atrial-cortical association was independent of LV mass and ejection fraction. C_LIO_LIExploratory: HbA1c related to LV end-diastolic volume differently by APOE {varepsilon}4 status. papers.title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis in adrenoleukodystrophy: a new piece in the puzzle?
papers.abstract: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is the most common monogenic disorder affecting brain white matter, presenting a broad clinical spectrum from slowly progressive adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN) to rapidly advancing cerebral demyelination. Factors influencing the variable disease expressivity remain poorly understood. We conducted shotgun metagenomic profiling of fecal samples from X-ALD patients and integrated these data with targeted plasma metabolomic analyses of amino acids and key metabolic intermediates. We identified distinct microbiome-associated metabolic signatures across X-ALD phenotypes. Notably, Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and Helicobacter apodemus abundance were significantly altered in AMN compared with childhood CALD patients. In parallel, X-ALD patients exhibited evidence of microbial metabolic remodeling characterized by altered amino acid metabolism, reduced folate biosynthetic potential, and enrichment of stress-adaptive pathways, including redox-associated functions, glyoxylate shunt activity, lipid A modification, lipopolysaccharide assembly, biofilm adhesin biosynthesis, and curli fiber production. Consistent with these microbial changes, plasma levels of branched-chain amino acids and methionine, as well as serum folate concentrations, were significantly reduced. Importantly, methionine levels showed an inverse correlation with neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations in patients with cerebral disease. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between gut microbial metabolic capacity and systemic metabolic alterations in X-ALD. Our results reinforce previous evidence implicating methionine metabolism in disease severity. Collectively, these data support a modulatory role of the microbiota-gut-brain axis in neuroinflammatory and mitochondrial-related processes underlying X-ALD progression and highlight new opportunities for biomarker development and microbiome-informed therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Too early for LATE? Age at onset is associated with the clinical and neuroimaging expression of limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 pathology in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC) frequently co-occurs with Alzheimers disease (AD) pathology and has been studied mainly in older populations. We examined its frequency and expression in 196 individuals with autopsy-confirmed intermediate-to-high AD neuropathologic change, enriched for younger-onset cases, integrating neuropathology with antemortem clinical, cognitive and neuroimaging data. LATE-NC occurred in 31% overall and 19% of individuals with symptom onset [≤]65 years. Its frequency increased with older age at symptom onset, and its presence was associated with greater episodic memory impairment and smaller amygdala and hippocampal volumes. Among individuals with LATE-NC, older age at symptom onset was associated with memory-first presentation and greater medial temporal involvement, including higher inferior-to-medial temporal metabolism ratios on FDG PET. Despite its lower frequency, LATE-NC co-pathology should still be considered in early-onset AD, where selected clinical features and neuroimaging markers described in older populations may be less applicable.

papers.title: Persistent gut microbiota alterations after ischemic stroke are modifiable by probiotic intervention
papers.abstract: The gut-brain axis has emerged as a critical modulator in neurological diseases, including stroke. While acute post-stroke dysbiosis is well established, it remains unclear whether these alterations persist long-term and can be therapeutically modulated. This study addresses this gap through integrated metagenomic and metabolomic profiling in two independent clinical stroke cohorts, complemented by experimental models. Experimental stroke induced persistent changes in gut microbiota composition and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. In patients, microbiota composition remained distinct from controls up to three months after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), accompanied by persistent reductions in propionic and valeric acid and reduced abundance of Prevotella-associated microbial signatures. We performed a randomized, double-blind interventional trial (PRISE) testing a multispecies probiotic versus placebo, using household members as additional controls. Probiotic intervention led to microbiome compositional changes with increased abundance of beneficial taxa and significantly improved functional recovery. The tested probiotic strains showed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in vitro. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the microbiome represents a promising therapeutic avenue to improve chronic stroke recovery, warranting validation in larger Phase III clinical trials.

papers.title: Renovascular hypertension drives ischemic white matter injury via brain endothelial AT1R signaling
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDWhite matter hyperintensities (WMHs), the principal imaging manifestation of cerebral small vessel disease, lack an animal model that produces pathology of sufficient magnitude to validate potential therapeutics. We characterized white matter (WM) degeneration in a renovascular hypertension (RVH) rat model, interrogated its mechanism, and tested its relevance in patients. METHODSRVH was induced by two-kidney, two-clip surgery and assessed by T2-weighted and diffusion MRI, myelin and axonal histology, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage markers. The influence of angiotensin II (Ang II) on barrier function in brain endothelial cells was examined using transendothelial electrical resistance and reactive oxygen species (ROS) assays. Losartan was infused intracerebroventricularly to block brain AT1R (Ang II type 1 receptor) without systemic blood pressure reduction. WMH burden was compared between patients with and without renal artery stenosis, and WMH progression across antihypertensive classes was assessed in the CHALLENGE (Korea), MSS2 (UK), LBC1936 (UK), and SPRINT-MIND-MRI (US) cohorts. RESULTSApproximately two-thirds of RVH rats developed WMHs that expanded between 7 and 9 weeks, accompanied by reduced fractional anisotropy, demyelination, axonal and mature oligodendrocyte loss, and glial activation. IgG, albumin, and fibrinogen leakage was confined to affected WM. Ang II impaired endothelial barrier function and generated ROS through AT1R. Intracerebroventricular losartan attenuated WM pathology and improved behavior while blood pressure remained comparably elevated. Patients with renal artery stenosis had higher WMH volumes (10.52 versus 6.52 mL; P = 0.035). Angiotensin receptor blocker use was associated with the slowest tertile of annual WMH progression in the Korean cohort (OR, 2.57 [95% CI, 1.20-5.61]) and among White participants in SPRINT-MIND-MRI (OR, 3.52 [95% CI, 1.05-12.29]). CONCLUSIONSRVH produces prominent ischemic WM degeneration driven by AT1R signaling, identifying a blood pressure-independent therapeutic target with corroborating clinical evidence.

papers.title: Interictal functional ultrasound imaging in human epilepsy resection and responsive neurostimulation surgery
papers.abstract: Over 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to medication and may require surgical or neuromodulation-based intervention. Accurate localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZ) and assessment of treatment-associated brain responses remain major clinical challenges. Current workflows may involve invasive intracranial monitoring, prolonged hospitalization, adjustment of anti-seizure medications, and seizure capture to localize the SOZ, while opportunities for complementary intraoperative functional assessment remain limited. We used intraoperative functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) to characterize interictal (i.e., non-seizure) cortical activity in nine patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and to assess treatment-associated brain responses following SOZ resection and responsive neurostimulation (RNS). fUSI signals were acquired directly from the exposed cortex during standard-of-care surgery. We developed six ultrafast power Doppler-based interictal activity markers (IaMs) to distinguish SOZ from peri-resection zone (PRZ) cortex and to quantify treatment-associated changes. The IaMs revealed distinct interictal hemodynamic dynamics between SOZ and PRZ cortex. Following SOZ resection, all six markers changed significantly within the surrounding PRZ. RNS also induced robust, stimulation paradigm-dependent modulation of cortical hemodynamic dynamics. Notably, RNS and surgical resection produced concordant directional changes across five of the six IaMs, despite representing fundamentally different therapeutic interventions. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of intraoperative fUSI for characterizing and distinguishing interictal dynamics within SOZ and PRZ cortex and assessing treatment-associated cortical responses during human epilepsy surgery. Furthermore, fUSI could provide a complementary high-resolution functional imaging approach alongside established clinical methods for SOZ localization and intraoperative functional assessment.
